Joshua is an assistant that runs entirely on your own computer, a Mac or a Linux PC. It searches the web, reads your files, writes code, makes pictures and learns how you like answers, without sending your life to anyone's servers.
Copy
Paste it in a terminal. A Mac with Apple Silicon (M1 or later) or a Linux PC, 8 GB of memory, 10–40 GB of free disk. On Linux an NVIDIA graphics card makes it much faster. Free and open.
install.sh
joshua.earth
AI at kilometre zero

Joshua is artificial intelligence on a human scale. It runs on the computer you already own, on a small model, with the power of the machine on your desk instead of a data centre's. No tech giant sits in the middle holding your data and setting the rules. Technology at the service of people and of the planet, not the other way round. Read the manifesto
The honest small print: the models were trained in data centres, and your computer uses electricity too. What changes is the scale, and who is in control.
Manifesto
Why it lives on your computer
> Your questions are yours

What you ask an assistant is a diary of your worries, your work and your plans. With Joshua, the model runs on your own chip. Your chats, files and memory sit in one folder on your disk, in plain files you can open, copy or delete.
> No profile, same answers

When Joshua searches the web it goes out anonymously, with no account and no cookies, so nobody builds a profile from it. The same question gets the same results on any computer, in the language you asked in.
> It works when the network doesn't
Untick the internet and Joshua keeps working: on a train, in the mountains, during an outage. Nothing switches off because a company changed its plans or its prices.
> You can see how it works, and change it

Every rule Joshua follows is in a few readable Python files. The memory it keeps about you is a notes file you can edit. And you can teach it your own style, on your own computer, with your own examples.

What you give up. A model that fits on a laptop is smaller than the giant ones in data centres: it makes more mistakes and writes less brilliantly. Joshua makes up for part of it by checking the web before it answers and fact-checking itself against its sources, and it tells you where each fact came from. It is also slower, and it needs a reasonably recent computer. If yours is too small, you can choose a cloud model for the chats that need one: see where your data lives.

Using a cloud model

Connect. Say yes to cloud models when you install, or later open ☁ Cloud models in Joshua and press Connect. A page on ollama.com opens: create an account (Continue with Google works) or sign in, and approve your computer.

Pay per use, a little at a time. New Ollama accounts pay per use: you add credit on ollama.com, with no subscription. That money pays Ollama for the computing power of its servers; Joshua itself is free and gets none of it. Gemma 4 31B, which also sees images and which Joshua sets up for you, is one of the cheapest: well under a cent per message, so a few dollars last a long time. Some older accounts still have a small free monthly allowance. Bigger models cost more per message; if you use them a lot, a plan such as Pro ($20 a month with $60 of use included) works out cheaper.

Add a model. Choose ＋ Add a model… at the bottom of the model menu under the prompt (or open ☁ Cloud models), pick one from the list (👁 means it can also see images) and press Add to the model menu. Nothing is downloaded.
Choose it per chat. Pick the ☁ model under the prompt. Joshua starts every new chat on your local model, so the cloud is always a choice you make.
Plans and prices as of November 2026, from ollama.com/pricing; Ollama may change them. Local models stay free and unlimited.
Abilities
What Joshua does
Researches first
For facts that change, it searches, reads the pages, answers with numbered sources, then fact-checks its own answer against them.
Reads your files
Drop in text, Word, PDF or images. Each chat has its own folder; point a chat at a project folder and it works there.

Any model you like

Download other local models that fit your computer from inside Joshua, keep them up to date, or pick a bigger cloud model for a chat. On macOS 26 Joshua can also use Apple Intelligence, the model built into the Mac.
Works with your apps
A built-in API in the common OpenAI format lets your scripts, a robot or other apps use Joshua, tools and memory included, from this computer or your home network. How to use it
Keeps going

Goal mode works until a task is done and checked. Swarm mode asks several agents and merges the best answer. Scheduled tasks run on their own at set times, while Joshua is open and the computer is on. More
Ways of working
More than questions and answers
🎯 Goal mode

Give Joshua a goal instead of a question. It plans, uses its tools, checks the result and keeps going, round after round up to the limit you set, until it marks the goal as done or tells you why it can't. “Read the three PDFs in this chat and write a one-page comparison as a Word file.”
🐝 Swarm mode

Several agents work on the same request at once, each in its own way: one methodical, one sceptical, one practical. Joshua then compares their answers, checks the facts they disagree on and writes one final answer. Slower, better on hard or open questions. “What are the strongest arguments for and against a four-day week?”
🕒 Scheduled tasks

Ask Joshua to do something at a set time: once, every day, every week or every few hours. Each run appears as a new ⏰ chat. “Every morning at 8, summarise the news about artificial intelligence.” Tasks run while Joshua is open and the computer is on.
💭 Deep thinking
The model reasons step by step before it answers, and you can read its reasoning. Slower, but better at maths, logic and problems with many parts. Switch it on only when a question needs it.
Install
One line, a few questions

The installer looks at your computer first: chip, graphics card, memory, free disk, and estimates how fast each model would run on it. It asks whether you want deep thinking, images and fine-tuning, or cloud models only, shows the plan and the space it needs, and waits for your yes.

Then it installs Ollama, the engine that runs the models, a private copy of Python, Joshua and the models you chose, and offers to start Joshua when you log in, so it opens at once and scheduled tasks can run. On a Mac, Joshua is an app of its own in the Applications folder, with its own window and Dock icon; on Linux it opens in its own window from the applications menu. Everything else stays in one folder, ~/AskJoshua, with an uninstall.sh that removes it.

Before you start. Installing takes about 20 minutes, most of it downloading, depending on your connection and the options you choose. On some Macs, macOS also offers to install Apple's “Command Line Developer Tools” along the way: let it finish. Its first time estimate (sometimes many hours) is wrong; it usually takes 10–20 minutes. Cloud models need an Ollama account: when the installer opens the sign-in page, Continue with Google with your Gmail address is enough. New Ollama accounts pay per use: add a few dollars of credit on ollama.com before using cloud models. Local models are always free. Local models need no account.
Prefer to read before you run? Open install.sh: it is plain, commented shell. All of Joshua's code is on GitHub, under the AGPL licence.

Fine-tuning
Teach Joshua your style

Fine-tuning nudges a few of the model's billions of numbers with your examples, so it picks up a habit: a tone of voice, a format, your jargon. Joshua walks you through it in the Teach Joshua panel, explaining each step as you go. It runs on your Mac in 15 to 60 minutes, and your examples never leave it.

Not the same as “customising” ChatGPT or Claude. In those apps, custom GPTs and Projects hand the model your documents and instructions to read before it answers. The model itself stays the same, and it stays on their servers. Fine-tuning changes the model. Joshua trains a LoRA adapter: a few million new numbers, next to the model's billions, learned from your examples and then merged into a new copy of the model that belongs to you.

Why small models. A small model knows less and reasons less well than the giants. But it can be retrained on a laptop in an hour, copied and run anywhere, so it can become a specialist in your tone, your formats, your field's jargon. That kind of flexibility is out of reach with a model you can only rent.

It teaches style, not facts. Train it on 200 answers about your company and it will sound like it knows your company, but it will invent the details. For facts, Joshua has memory, your files and the web.
Name itEach fine-tune is a project. The result is a new model called joshua-<name>.
Examples100–500 pairs of what you say and the answer you want. Upload a file, pick past chats, or write them.
TrainA LoRA adapter learns from them with mlx-lm. A live chart shows when it learns and when it starts memorising.
CompareAsk the same new question before and after, side by side.
InstallMerged, converted to GGUF, added to Ollama, and listed in Joshua's model menu.
Inside
How Joshua thinks

The model has no memory of its own. Every time you write, Joshua sends it the whole conversation, and the model either answers or asks for a tool. Joshua runs the tool, adds the result, and asks again, up to 25 rounds.
1 · The chatInstructions, your messages, every tool result.
2 · The modelqwen3-vl in Ollama reads all of it and replies.
3 · Tools?No: the answer is shown. Yes: go on.
4 · Run toolsSearch, read, code, files, images. Results go back to 1.
Built with Ollama · qwen3-vl · FLUX.2 klein via mflux · mlx-lm · llama.cpp's converter · Gradio · anonymous search through ddgs. All open source.

How-to · Joshua API

Talk to Joshua
from your own programs

Joshua has a built-in API: your scripts, a robot, a home-automation box or any app that works with “OpenAI-compatible” servers can send it a question and get an answer back. Every request runs the full Joshua, with web research, tools and memory, on your computer.
Get started First request Python JavaScript Pictures Options Other devices Reference Privacy
Get started
Open Joshua. The API starts with it, at http://127.0.0.1:7861/v1.
In the right column, open 🔌 API. It shows the address, your key and a ready-made command to try.
Copy the key. Every request must carry it, like a password. Only your computer knows it; Make a new key replaces it if it ever leaks.
Joshua must be running for the API to answer. The key is stored in ~/AskJoshua/joshua/api.json.
Your first request
In Terminal, list the models you can use, then ask a question. Replace YOUR-KEY with the key from the panel.
terminal
The answer comes back in the standard format; the text is in choices[0].message.content:
answer
Joshua may search the web, read pages or run code before answering, so a reply can take from a few seconds to a few minutes, depending on the question and your computer.
Python
The easiest way is the official openai library: point it at Joshua instead of OpenAI.
python · openai
Or with plain requests, for example on a Raspberry Pi robot that keeps the conversation going by sending the history back each time:
python · requests
JavaScript
javascript
A web page on another site can't call Joshua directly; run this in Node or in your own app.
Sending pictures
Send a photo as a data: URL inside the message. With a model that sees images (qwen3-vl does), Joshua looks at it directly; otherwise it uses its local image tool.
python
You can give Joshua extra instructions with a system message: they are added after Joshua's own. And you can ask it not to save the exchange as a chat:
Field
What it does
model
joshua = your default local model. Or any name from /v1/models, such as qwen3-vl:8b-instruct. Cloud models (ending in cloud) are used only if you name one.
messages
The conversation: system, user and assistant messages, oldest first. Joshua keeps no state between requests, so send the history you want it to remember.
stream
true works with clients that expect streaming, but the whole answer arrives in one piece at the end.
joshua_save
false = don't save this exchange as a 🔌 chat. Default true.
From other devices
By default only programs on the same computer can connect. To use Joshua from a robot, a phone or another computer at home:
In 🔌 API, tick Allow other devices on my network.
Restart Joshua (run ~/AskJoshua/stop.sh, then open Joshua again).
The panel now shows your computer's network address, such as http://192.168.1.20:7861/v1. Use that address on the other device, with the same key.
Keep it to your home network. Don't open port 7861 on your router: the key protects Joshua, but the connection is not encrypted.
Reference
Request
GET /v1/models
Lists joshua and every installed model that can use tools. owned_by says this computer or cloud.
POST /v1/chat/completions
Runs Joshua on the messages and returns its answer, in the OpenAI chat format.
Error
Meaning
The key is missing or wrong. Send Authorization: Bearer YOUR-KEY.
Something in the request is wrong, such as an unknown model name. The message explains what.
connection refused
Joshua isn't running, or (from another device) “Allow other devices” is off or Joshua hasn't been restarted.
Need only the bare model, without Joshua's tools and memory? Ollama has its own API at http://127.0.0.1:11434, also OpenAI-compatible at /v1, with no key.
Privacy
With a local model, requests are answered entirely on your computer.
Every request is saved as a 🔌 chat in Joshua, so you can always see what programs asked, unless the program sends joshua_save: false.
API requests don't add to Joshua's memory about you, but local models can use your memory notes to answer.
A cloud model is used only if a program asks for one by name; then the conversation goes to Ollama's servers, as described in where your data lives.

Joshua Manifesto
Manifesto

An intelligence
you own
Why Joshua exists, what it promises, and where it falls short.
Why Principles In practice Joshua and the Yattaphone Join
Why

Our computers and phones are the most intimate objects we own. They know where we sleep, who we love, what we fear, what we search for at three in the morning. Now an artificial intelligence sits between us and them: it reads our documents, listens to our questions, remembers what we tell it. We ask it things we would not ask a friend.

Almost always, that intelligence lives on someone else's servers. Its rules change without asking, and our conversations flow to places we will never see. We are not its owners. We are its tenants, and the rent is our private life.
Whoever controls that intelligence will know us better than we know ourselves. It should be us.
Joshua is a small attempt at the other way: an assistant that lives on your own computer, that you can read, change and switch off. Not a service. A tool that is yours.
Principles
Who runs it, owns it. An assistant that lives on someone else's computer works for someone else. Joshua runs on yours.
Understanding is freedom. Every part of Joshua can be read, explained and changed. No black boxes, no magic, no “trust us”.
Privacy is a right, not a setting. It is not a switch buried in a menu. It is the default, and nobody has to ask for it.
Our data stays with us. What Joshua learns about you lives on your computer, in files you can open. Nothing leaves without your knowledge.
The intelligence must serve its owner. It answers to you: no advertiser, no account, no one watching. It uses outside services only when you choose, and can always be switched off.
Slower, smaller, ours. We accept a model that is smaller, slower and sometimes wrong, in exchange for one that is ours and keeps working without anyone's permission.
Shared, not sold. Joshua is free, and how it works is published, mistakes included, so that anyone can build on it. Knowledge kept closed is power kept by few.
In practice
Principles are cheap. This is what they mean, part by part.
Open models, chosen for your computer. The installer looks at your memory and chip and downloads models that fit. You can add others, or remove them, whenever you like.

One engine, named openly. The models run on Ollama, free software on your computer. If you choose one of its cloud models for a chat, that conversation goes to Ollama's servers, and Joshua marks it clearly. What stays local and what doesn't.
Everything in one folder. Chats, files, memory and settings are plain files in ~/AskJoshua. You can read them, copy them, back them up or delete them.
Code you can read. Joshua is a handful of Python files, installed as they are and published on GitHub under the AGPL licence. Open them, change them, ask Joshua to explain them.
Answers that show their sources. When Joshua searches the web, it tells you where each fact came from, so you can check it.
Taught on your machine. You can teach Joshua your style with your own examples. The training happens on your computer, and the result stays there.

Honest about limits. A model that fits on a laptop makes more mistakes than the giants in data centres. It needs a reasonably recent computer. Scheduled tasks run only while the computer is on and Joshua is open. We write that down too.
Joshua and the Yattaphone

This manifesto began as the Yattaphone's: a phone you build yourself from a Raspberry Pi and parts anyone can buy, documented step by step. A phone you own needs an assistant you own. Joshua is that assistant: first on the computer, and one day, we hope, on the phone itself, without depending on anyone else's servers.
Same idea, two devices: your hardware, your data, your intelligence.
Join
Joshua is not finished, and never will be. That is the point.
Install it. Then tell us where it was wrong.

Share what you learn. Every problem solved in public is one less problem for the next person.
We are not asking you to trust another company with your thoughts. We are asking you to keep them.

Who
Joshua is made by Fabio De Ponte, a journalist who reports on artificial intelligence and teaches other journalists how to use it.

He is doing a PhD on how language emerges among AI agents, at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel and the University of Namur, and holds an MSc in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence from Goldsmiths, University of London. He wrote critical biographies of Steve Jobs and Bill Gates.
He also builds the Yattaphone, a phone you make yourself from a Raspberry Pi.
The personal computer came with a simple promise: the machine on your desk is yours. Artificial intelligence is moving the other way, into the data centres of a few companies.

Joshua is an attempt to bring it back to the desk: small enough to run at home, open enough to understand, simple enough to install without being an engineer. It is not a company and it sells nothing. The manifesto says the rest.
How it is made

Joshua is written with the help of AI coding assistants and tested on ordinary Macs, from an 8 GB M1 to a 16 GB M4. It stands on the work of others: Ollama, the Qwen models, Gradio, mlx and many more. Every line of Joshua's own code is on GitHub.

Write to info@joshua.earth. For bugs and ideas, open an issue on GitHub.
